stem: Eight months into tamoxifen, a 55-year-old reports new vaginal bleeding. What should happen?

options.C: Add estrogen to stabilize the lining

why: Tamoxifen’s endometrial agonism raises hyperplasia/cancer risk — new bleeding needs prompt evaluation.
discriminator: Raloxifene would not carry this risk.

stem: A 66-year-old on isosorbide mononitrate for angina requests tadalafil. What should the PA do?
why: Nitrates and PDE5 inhibitors both raise NO/cGMP; together, life-threatening hypotension — an absolute contraindication.
discriminator: Riociguat is also contraindicated with PDE5 inhibitors.

stem: A 38-year-old who smokes daily asks for contraception. Which choice is most appropriate?

options.C: Combined pill at the lowest dose

why: Smoking with age over 35 substantially raises estrogen’s thromboembolic risk; progestin-only methods carry no estrogen.
takeaway: Smoker > 35, VTE history, migraine with aura → progestin-only.
discriminator: When estrogen is off the table, progestin-only is the right first choice.

stem: A patient with pulmonary hypertension on riociguat asks for tadalafil for ED. Best answer?
why: PDE5 inhibitors are contraindicated with nitrates or riociguat.
discriminator: Same cGMP logic as nitrates.

stem: Why does tamoxifen raise endometrial cancer risk while raloxifene largely does not?
why: SERMs act as agonists in some tissues and antagonists in others; tamoxifen activates the endometrium, raloxifene is essentially neutral.
takeaway: Both: breast antagonist, bone agonist, VTE. Only tamoxifen: endometrium.
discriminator: Tissue-selective agonism, not a class effect.

stem: A woman with PCOS on metformin is scheduled for a CT with iodinated contrast and has reduced kidney function. Advice?
why: Hold metformin for an iodinated contrast study or renal impairment (lactic acidosis).
discriminator: GI upset early; take with meals.

stem: A man on testosterone injections has a hematocrit of 56%. What is the issue?
why: Testosterone causes erythrocytosis; monitor hematocrit and PSA; oral forms risk hepatotoxicity; suppresses fertility.
discriminator: Contraindicated in prostate cancer and pregnancy.

stem: A patient on sildenafil starts clarithromycin. What should be anticipated?
why: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, clarithromycin) raise PDE5 inhibitor levels.
takeaway: CYP3A4 inhibitor + PDE5 → lower the dose.
discriminator: Nitrates remain absolutely contraindicated.

stem: A woman on anastrozole asks how to protect her bones. Best advice?
why: Aromatase inhibitors cause bone loss and joint pain; bisphosphonates and calcium with vitamin D protect bone.
discriminator: Postmenopausal use only.

stem: What distinguishes tamsulosin from doxazosin?
why: Tamsulosin/silodosin are uroselective; doxazosin/terazosin lower BP more; all share orthostatic hypotension and a first-dose effect.
takeaway: Selectivity changes degree, not the class risk.
discriminator: Floppy iris syndrome in cataract surgery.

stem: A patient on the progestin-only pill took today’s dose 4 hours late. What counseling applies?

options.A: Stop the pill for a week
options.E: Switch to a combined pill now

why: Norethindrone’s efficacy falls if a dose is more than 3 hours late; taken daily with no pill-free days.
discriminator: Ectopic risk if it fails.

stem: How do bicalutamide and finasteride differ in reducing androgen action?
why: Flutamide/bicalutamide are direct AR blockers (prostate cancer, with a GnRH agonist); finasteride/dutasteride block testosterone → DHT.
discriminator: Same drugs (5-ARIs) return for BPH.

stem: A patient on warfarin starts tamoxifen. What should be anticipated?
why: Testosterone and tamoxifen raise INR with warfarin.
discriminator: Tamoxifen also raises VTE risk.

stem: A man on tamsulosin is scheduled for cataract surgery. What should be done?

options.B: Switch to finasteride the day before

why: Floppy iris syndrome is a recognized intraoperative complication with alpha1 blockers — preoperative reconciliation.
takeaway: Alpha1 blocker + cataract surgery → flag it.
discriminator: Also orthostasis, first-dose effect.

stem: A woman who had a hysterectomy wants estrogen for hot flashes. Does she need a progestin?
why: The progestin protects the endometrium; after hysterectomy estrogen alone is acceptable.
discriminator: Still screen for VTE risk.

stem: A man on tamsulosin (no nitrates) wants sildenafil. What is the remaining concern?
why: Alpha1 blockade and NO-cGMP potentiation both lower BP — less severe than nitrates but warrants spacing or monitoring.
discriminator: Tadalafil profile allows tamsulosin 0.4 mg with caution.

stem: A man on finasteride lives with his pregnant wife. Key counseling?

options.E: She can crush them for him

why: 5-ARIs can cause ambiguous genitalia in a male fetus; pregnant partners avoid crushed or broken tablets.
discriminator: PSA halved on therapy.

stem: A 79-year-old with mild cognitive impairment becomes confused weeks after starting oxybutynin. Best change?
why: Oxybutynin has the highest CNS anticholinergic burden; mirabegron relaxes the detrusor via beta3 with no anticholinergic activity.
discriminator: Review all anticholinergics (diphenhydramine, TCAs).

stem: Which receptor–location pair drives voiding?
why: Parasympathetic ACh at M3 contracts the detrusor; sympathetic alpha1 closes the neck and beta3 relaxes the detrusor during storage.
discriminator: M2 is abundant but contributes less.
src: L12 S5; S7; S9; SG U6-R11

stem: Why do alpha1 blockers for BPH cause orthostatic hypotension?

options.B: They act only in the bladder

why: Alpha1 blockade at the bladder neck also lowers systemic vascular resistance — orthostasis and a first-dose effect.
takeaway: Same receptor family as the Unit 5 antihypertensives.
discriminator: Give the first dose of doxazosin at bedtime.

stem: A patient with poorly controlled hypertension needs OAB therapy. What is the concern with mirabegron?
why: Mirabegron can raise blood pressure — monitor in uncontrolled hypertension; it also inhibits CYP2D6.
takeaway: Mirabegron: no anticholinergic burden, but watch BP.
discriminator: Can combine with an antimuscarinic for refractory OAB.

stem: A woman with PCOS on spironolactone for hirsutism plans to conceive. Key counseling?

options.C: Continue; it is safe in pregnancy

why: Spironolactone blocks the androgen receptor; avoid in pregnancy (feminization of a male fetus).
discriminator: Also hyperkalemia with ACEi/ARB or potassium.

stem: Which pairing of drug and mechanism is correct?
why: Mirabegron beta3; oxybutynin M3 (and M2) antagonist; tamsulosin alpha1; finasteride 5-ARI; sildenafil PDE5.
takeaway: One receptor, one location, one class.
discriminator: Metformin in PCOS works through insulin.

stem: A patient with dementia on donepezil is started on oxybutynin. What is the problem?
why: Cholinesterase inhibitors oppose antimuscarinics, and oxybutynin adds CNS anticholinergic burden.
discriminator: Mirabegron is the alternative.

stem: Which drug interaction blunts tamoxifen’s activation?
why: CYP2D6 inhibitors (paroxetine, fluoxetine) blunt tamoxifen activation.
discriminator: Tamoxifen also raises INR with warfarin.

stem: A woman with PCOS and a BMI of 36 has not improved on metformin. Which emerging option fits?
why: GLP-1 receptor agonists are increasingly used off-label in PCOS with obesity (weight loss, insulin sensitization).
discriminator: Usually combined with other therapy.

stem: A 54-year-old with an intact uterus starts estradiol for vasomotor symptoms. What else is required?
why: Unopposed estrogen with a uterus drives endometrial proliferation → hyperplasia and cancer; a progestin counters it.
discriminator: After hysterectomy, estrogen alone is fine.

stem: What is the central mechanism linking insulin resistance to hyperandrogenism in PCOS?
why: Hyperinsulinemia directly stimulates theca-cell androgen production and lowers hepatic SHBG, raising free testosterone.
takeaway: Insulin → androgens → worse insulin resistance (a cycle).
discriminator: Explains why metabolic therapy helps reproductive symptoms.

stem: A man with metastatic prostate cancer starts leuprolide. Which antiandrogen is often added?
why: Flutamide/bicalutamide are pure AR blockers, often combined with a GnRH agonist (tumor-flare prevention).
discriminator: Flutamide: gynecomastia, hepatotoxicity.

stem: Which adverse effect is most associated with sildenafil?
why: PDE5 inhibitors cause headache, flushing, dyspepsia and visual disturbance (blue tinge, notably sildenafil).
discriminator: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors raise PDE5 inhibitor levels.

stem: Which adverse effect of estrogen therapy is most tested?
why: Estrogen’s VTE risk rises with smoking, age over 35 and VTE history.
discriminator: Raises hepatic clotting factors (textbook).

stem: Which adverse-effect cluster follows from antimuscarinic OAB therapy?
why: Systemic muscarinic blockade causes dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision and confusion; avoid in narrow-angle glaucoma and retention.
takeaway: Can’t see, can’t spit, can’t poop, can’t think.
discriminator: Burden is cumulative across all drugs.

stem: Which receptor does the external urethral sphincter use?
why: Somatic (pudendal) nicotinic control holds the external sphincter.
discriminator: Voluntary relaxation during voiding.

stem: Why is metformin called an indirect therapy for hyperandrogenism in PCOS?
why: Metformin improves insulin sensitivity and reduces hyperinsulinemia’s stimulation of ovarian androgens — no hormone receptor involved.
discriminator: GI upset; hold for contrast or renal impairment.

stem: A postmenopausal woman with osteoporosis and no breast cancer wants a SERM. Which fits?
why: Raloxifene is a bone agonist, endometrium-neutral — preferred for osteoporosis prevention without a breast cancer indication.
discriminator: Both SERMs raise VTE.

stem: A man with BPH wants quick relief and a smaller prostate long term. Best regimen?
why: Alpha1 blockers act in days; 5-ARIs shrink the prostate over 3–6 months — frequently combined.
discriminator: 5-ARI: PSA halved; pregnant partners avoid crushed tablets.

stem: Why do finasteride and dutasteride appear in both GU sessions?
why: 5-ARIs block testosterone → DHT: hirsutism/alopecia in Session 1, BPH in Session 2.
discriminator: PSA halved — double it.

stem: How do PDE5 inhibitors produce an erection?

options.B: They block alpha1 in the penis

why: NANC nerves release NO → cGMP → smooth-muscle relaxation; PDE5 inhibitors prolong cGMP.
takeaway: No stimulation, no signal to prolong.
discriminator: Tadalafil has the longest half-life.

stem: A patient with migraine with aura wants contraception that also lightens heavy periods. Best fit?
why: Migraine with aura rules out estrogen; the LNG IUD is progestin-only and treats heavy menstrual bleeding.
discriminator: Check strings; perforation and expulsion risks.

stem: A man on dutasteride for 2 years has a PSA of 2.1 ng/mL. How should it be interpreted?
why: 5-ARIs lower PSA by roughly half on long-term therapy; adjust when interpreting.
discriminator: Onset of benefit 3–6 months.

stem: A 42-year-old premenopausal woman with ER-positive breast cancer asks about letrozole alone. Best answer?

options.C: It raises estrogen to fight tumor

why: Aromatase inhibitors block peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogen; before menopause the ovary dominates (needs ovarian suppression).
discriminator: Protect bone: calcium, vitamin D, bisphosphonate.

stem: Which PDE5 inhibitor has the longest half-life, allowing flexible dosing?
why: Tadalafil has a longer half-life and more flexible dosing.
discriminator: Sildenafil = blue vision.

stem: A 25-year-old with PCOS, irregular cycles and hirsutism (BMI 32) does not want pregnancy. Best plan?
why: Contraception for immediate symptom control; metformin for the metabolic driver and long-term diabetes risk.
discriminator: GLP-1 agonists: off-label with obesity.

stem: How do estrogens produce their effects on the endometrium, bone and lipids?
why: Estrogens bind intracellular ER-alpha/ER-beta and regulate gene transcription in reproductive, bone, cardiovascular and CNS tissue.
discriminator: Effects: endometrial proliferation, bone density, ↑ HDL ↓ LDL.

stem: A man on testosterone gel lives with young children. Key counseling?

options.B: Apply it to the hands only

why: Testosterone gels risk secondary exposure; also monitor hematocrit, PSA, lipids.
discriminator: Contraindicated in prostate cancer.

stem: While counseling a patient, you learn his wife has new vaginal bleeding on tamoxifen. What do you advise?
why: Tamoxifen’s endometrial agonism raises hyperplasia/cancer risk; new bleeding warrants prompt evaluation.
discriminator: The U6 integrated case pulls Session 1 into Session 2.

stem: A patient with narrow-angle glaucoma needs OAB treatment. Which class is preferred?
why: Antimuscarinics can worsen narrow-angle glaucoma and urinary retention; mirabegron has no anticholinergic activity.
discriminator: Mirabegron can raise BP.

stem: A woman on a combined pill starts rifampin for latent TB. What counseling is needed?

options.A: Switch rifampin to St. John’s wort

why: Enzyme inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St. John’s wort) lower combined contraceptive efficacy.
discriminator: Textbook: rifampin speeds estrogen/progestin metabolism.

stem: During storage, what does norepinephrine do at alpha1 and beta3 receptors?

options.A: Contracts the detrusor and opens the neck

why: Alpha1 at the bladder neck contracts (continence); beta3 on the detrusor relaxes (low-pressure filling).
takeaway: Alpha1 = door shut; beta3 = tank relaxed.
discriminator: Both become drug targets: tamsulosin and mirabegron.

stem: Which adverse effect is specific to long-term depot medroxyprogesterone (DMPA)?
why: DMPA carries a boxed warning for loss of bone mineral density with prolonged use.
discriminator: Progestin-only methods also cause irregular bleeding early.
